Carrot.explanation: Carrots are orange and help make your eyes strong and healthy
points: Rich in beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A essential for vision
The orange color comes from high levels of carotenoids, powerful antioxidants
Originally purple in Afghanistan; orange variety developed in 17th-century Netherlands
Can be eaten raw, cooked, juiced, or as baby carrots (peeled and shaped)
Leaves and stems are also edible and used in some cuisines

Broccoli.explanation: Broccoli looks like tiny trees and is packed with vitamins
points: Belongs to the cabbage family (Brassicaceae) and is a cruciferous vegetable
Very high in vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, and fiber
Contains sulforaphane, a compound studied for potential cancer-fighting properties
The edible part is actually the flower buds before they open
Purple and white varieties exist alongside the common green

Tomato.explanation: Tomatoes are actually a fruit but we eat them like a vegetable
points: Botanically a berry (fruit) because it develops from the ovary of a flower
Classified as a vegetable for culinary and legal purposes in many countries
Major source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant linked to heart health
Thousands of varieties exist — cherry, beefsteak, plum, heirloom, etc.
Native to western South America; introduced to Europe in the 16th century

Potato.explanation: Potatoes grow underground and can be made into many yummy dishes
points: World's fourth-largest food crop after maize, rice, and wheat
Starchy tuber that stores energy for the plant
Contains resistant starch when cooled (great for gut health)
Over 4,000 varieties worldwide with colors including purple, red, yellow
Ireland's Great Famine (1845–1852) was caused by potato blight

Corn.explanation: Each corn cob has hundreds of tiny yellow kernels on it
points: Also called maize — one of the most produced grains globally
Kernels are actually fruits (caryopses) on a cob (spike)
Sweet corn is harvested immature; field corn is dried for feed and products
Originated in Mexico ~9,000 years ago from teosinte plant
Corn silk (stigmas) is used in traditional medicine

Spinach.explanation: Spinach makes you strong and healthy just like Popeye the sailor
points: Extremely nutrient-dense — high in iron, vitamins A, C, K, folate, magnesium
Popeye association began in 1930s cartoons (partly due to iron myth)
Contains oxalates that can reduce calcium absorption
Eaten raw in salads or cooked (reduces oxalate content)
Native to Persia; spread to Europe in Middle Ages

Pea.explanation: Tiny green peas grow snugly inside a long green pod
points: Legume family — fixes nitrogen in soil like beans
Snow peas and snap peas are eaten whole with pod
Mendel used pea plants for his famous genetics experiments
High in protein, fiber, vitamin C, and vitamin K
Fresh, frozen, canned, or dried (split peas)

Cucumber.explanation: Cucumbers are cool and refreshing and mostly made of water
points: 95% water — excellent for hydration
Botanically a fruit (berry) like tomato and squash
Contains cucurbitacins — can taste bitter in stressed plants
Used in pickles, salads, spa treatments, and skincare
Native to India; cultivated for over 3,000 years

Pepper.explanation: Peppers come in red, yellow, orange, and green colors
points: Bell peppers are the mild, large variety; chili peppers are spicy
Color changes as they ripen — green → yellow/orange → red
Very high in vitamin C (more than oranges per weight)
Capsaicin in spicy peppers creates heat sensation
Native to Central and South America

Pumpkin.explanation: Pumpkins are big orange vegetables used to make jack-o-lanterns
points: Winter squash — large fruits of Cucurbita species
All parts edible: flesh, seeds (pepitas), flowers, leaves
High in beta-carotene, vitamin A, fiber
Used in pies, soups, Halloween carving, and livestock feed
Native to North America; cultivated for thousands of years

Onion.explanation: Onions make your eyes water when you cut them due to a special chemical
points: Syn-propanethial-S-oxide gas released when cut irritates eyes
Contains quercetin, a powerful antioxidant
Layers protect the bulb and store energy
Varieties: yellow, white, red, sweet, shallots, green onions
One of the oldest cultivated vegetables — over 7,000 years

Garlic.explanation: Garlic is used in cooking all over the world and is good for your health
points: Contains allicin — released when crushed, responsible for smell and benefits
Strong antimicrobial properties — used medicinally for centuries
High in sulfur compounds linked to heart health
Bulb is made of cloves; green shoots (garlic scapes) also edible
Native to Central Asia; used since ancient Egypt

Cauliflower.explanation: Cauliflower looks like a white version of broccoli and is very nutritious
points: Cruciferous vegetable — same family as broccoli and cabbage
High in vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, fiber
Colored varieties exist: purple, green, orange
Head is actually undeveloped flower buds
Very versatile — rice, pizza crust, mashed, roasted

Cabbage.explanation: Cabbages are round leafy vegetables that can be purple or green
points: Cruciferous — high in vitamin C, vitamin K, fiber
Fermented cabbage = sauerkraut (probiotic-rich)
Varieties: green, red/purple, Savoy, Napa/Chinese
Very hardy — stores well for months
Symbol of prosperity in some cultures

Eggplant.explanation: Eggplants are shiny purple vegetables also known as aubergine
points: Botanically a berry — nightshade family (like tomato, potato)
Sponge-like flesh absorbs flavors and oil when cooking
High in nasunin — antioxidant concentrated in purple skin
Common in Mediterranean, Indian, and Middle Eastern cuisine
Originally from India; name 'eggplant' from white egg-shaped varieties

Zucchini.explanation: Zucchinis are green summer squashes that grow very quickly
points: Summer squash — harvested immature while skin is tender
Grows extremely fast — can double in size overnight
Flowers are edible and considered a delicacy
Mild flavor — used raw, grilled, spiralized, or in bread
Yellow and striped varieties also common

Asparagus.explanation: Asparagus grows as tall spears and is one of the first vegetables to grow in spring
points: Perennial plant — produces for 15–20 years once established
High in folate, vitamin K, fiber, and antioxidants
Contains asparagine — gives urine distinctive smell in some people
White asparagus grown underground to prevent greening
Purple asparagus has higher antioxidant content

Celery.explanation: Celery makes a crunchy snack and is almost all water and fiber
points: 95% water — very low calorie (negative-calorie myth)
High in fiber, vitamin K, potassium
Seeds used as spice (celery seed)
Stalks, leaves, and root (celeriac) all edible
Ancient medicinal use for hypertension

Radish.explanation: Radishes are small spicy root vegetables that can be red or white
points: Cruciferous — fast-growing (ready in 3–4 weeks)
Spicy flavor from glucosinolates (same as mustard)
Varieties: red globe, daikon (large white), watermelon radish
Leaves are edible and nutritious
Used raw, pickled, or cooked

Beetroot.explanation: Beetroot turns your hands and tongue a bright red or purple color
points: Rich in nitrates — can help lower blood pressure
High in betalains — unique antioxidants giving red/purple color
Leaves (beet greens) more nutritious than root
Varieties: red, golden, white, striped (Chioggia)
Used in borscht, salads, and natural food coloring

Sweet Potato.explanation: Sweet potatoes are orange inside and packed with vitamins and nutrients
points: Not related to regular potato — different plant family
Extremely high in vitamin A (beta-carotene) — one of best sources
Varieties: orange, purple, white, yellow
Lower glycemic index than white potatoes
Used in pies, fries, mash, and desserts

Artichoke.explanation: The artichoke is actually a flower bud that we eat before it blooms
points: Edible flower bud of thistle family
Heart (base) is the prized part; leaves have edible flesh at base
High in fiber, antioxidants, and cynarin (aids liver function)
California produces ~99% of U.S. artichokes
Baby artichokes are fully edible (no choke)

Leek.explanation: Leeks look like giant green onions and taste mild and sweet when cooked
points: Milder, sweeter cousin of onion
Used in soups (vichyssoise), stews, and Welsh cuisine
High in vitamin K and manganese
White part most commonly used; green tops can be used for stock
National emblem of Wales

Kale.explanation: Kale is one of the most nutritious leafy green vegetables you can eat
points: Extremely nutrient-dense — high in vitamins A, C, K, antioxidants
Varieties: curly, lacinato (dinosaur), red Russian
Contains oxalates — cooking reduces them
Used raw in salads, chips, smoothies, soups
Ancient vegetable — grown by Greeks and Romans

Brussels Sprout.explanation: Brussels sprouts look like tiny cabbages and grow along a long thick stalk
points: Cruciferous — high in vitamin C, vitamin K, fiber
Contain sulforaphane and glucosinolates (cancer-fighting compounds)
Sweetens after first frost due to starch conversion
Grows in clusters along tall stalk
Name from Brussels, Belgium where they were widely cultivated

Turnip.explanation: Turnips are round white root vegetables with a slightly peppery taste
points: Root and greens both edible
Milder when young; stronger flavor when mature
High in vitamin C and fiber
Used in stews, roasts, mash, and pickles
Ancient vegetable — mentioned in Roman texts

Parsnip.explanation: Parsnips look like white carrots and taste sweet and nutty when roasted
points: Sweetness increases after frost (starch to sugar conversion)
Related to carrot and parsley
High in fiber, vitamin C, folate
Used in soups, roasts, purees
Popular in Europe before potato became dominant

Fennel.explanation: Fennel has a mild licorice flavor and every part of it can be eaten
points: All parts edible: bulb, stalks, fronds, seeds
Anethole gives licorice/anise flavor
High in vitamin C, fiber, potassium
Seeds used as spice and digestive aid
Used in Mediterranean and Indian cooking

Bok Choy.explanation: Bok choy is a Chinese cabbage with crunchy white stems and tender green leaves
points: Also called pak choi or Chinese white cabbage
High in vitamins A, C, K, calcium
Stems stay crunchy even when cooked
Used in stir-fries, soups, dumplings
Baby bok choy is smaller and more tender

Kohlrabi.explanation: Kohlrabi looks like a small alien spaceship and tastes like mild broccoli
points: Stem swells into edible bulb above ground
Crisp, juicy texture — mild cabbage/broccoli flavor
High in vitamin C and fiber
Eaten raw in salads or cooked
Name means 'cabbage turnip' in German

Watercress.explanation: Watercress grows in fresh water streams and is one of the oldest eaten leaf vegetables
points: Highest nutrient density score of any food (CDC study)
High in vitamin K, vitamin C, antioxidants
Peppery, slightly bitter flavor
Grows in clean flowing water — needs constant moisture
Used by ancient Greeks and Romans medicinally

Arugula.explanation: Arugula has a peppery spicy taste and is popular in salads
points: Also called rocket or rucola
High in vitamin K, vitamin A, folate
Peppery flavor from glucosinolates
Used raw in salads, on pizza, in pesto
Ancient Roman aphrodisiac

Swiss Chard.explanation: Swiss chard has dark green leaves with bright red, yellow, or white stems
points: Very high in vitamin K, vitamin A, magnesium
Stems and leaves both edible — stems often cooked separately
Rainbow chard has colorful stems
Related to beets
Used in Mediterranean and Italian cooking

Collard Greens.explanation: Collard greens are a staple of Southern cooking and very rich in calcium
points: High in calcium, vitamin K, vitamin A
Tough leaves — usually slow-cooked or braised
Traditional Southern dish with ham hock or bacon
Related to kale and cabbage
One of the oldest cultivated greens

Mustard Greens.explanation: Mustard greens taste spicy and peppery and are common in Asian cuisine
points: Very high in vitamin K, vitamin A, antioxidants
Spicy flavor from mustard oils
Used in Indian saag, Southern cooking, Chinese dishes
Young leaves milder and eaten raw
Seeds used to make mustard condiment

Okra.explanation: Okra is a green pod vegetable that gets sticky when cooked, great for thickening soups
points: Mucilage (sticky substance) when cooked — natural thickener
High in fiber, vitamin C, folate
Used in gumbo, bhindi masala, stews
Pods contain tiny seeds
Native to Africa; widely grown in warm climates

Bean Sprout.explanation: Bean sprouts are tiny germinated beans crunchy and fresh in stir-fries
points: Mung bean sprouts most common
High in vitamin C, low calorie
Crunchy texture preserved when lightly cooked
Used in Asian stir-fries, salads, spring rolls
Germination increases nutrient availability

Snow Pea.explanation: Snow peas are flat pods where you eat the whole pod crunchy and sweet
points: Eaten whole before peas fully develop
High in vitamin C, vitamin K, fiber
Sweet and crisp — no string in some varieties
Common in Chinese stir-fries
Related to garden peas

Green Bean.explanation: Green beans are long pods picked young and eaten whole cooked or raw
points: Also called snap beans or string beans
High in fiber, vitamin C, vitamin K
Stringless varieties now common
Used in casseroles, salads, stir-fries
Harvested immature — pods crisp

Butternut Squash.explanation: Butternut squash has a sweet nutty flavor and turns bright orange when ripe
points: Winter squash — high in vitamin A, vitamin C, fiber
Sweet, nutty flavor — excellent roasted
Smooth skin when ripe
Long storage life
Used in soups, pies, risottos

Acorn Squash.explanation: Acorn squash is shaped like an acorn and has sweet orange flesh
points: Dark green with orange flesh
High in vitamin A, vitamin C
Often stuffed and baked
Ridged shape — distinctive appearance
Smaller than many winter squashes

Delicata Squash.explanation: Delicata squash has cream and green striped skin that is edible when cooked
points: Thin, edible skin — no peeling needed
Sweet, creamy flesh — tastes like sweet potato
High in vitamin A
Popular in fall cooking
Small size — easy to handle

Romanesco.explanation: Romanesco is a striking bright green vegetable that forms a perfect natural fractal pattern
points: Natural fractal — self-similar spirals
Related to cauliflower and broccoli
Mild nutty flavor — crunchier than cauliflower
High in vitamin C
Visually stunning — used in gourmet presentations

Sunchoke.explanation: Sunchokes are also called Jerusalem artichokes and taste sweet and nutty
points: Tubers of sunflower plant
High in inulin — prebiotic fiber
Sweet, nutty flavor — good raw or cooked
Not related to artichokes
Can cause gas in some people (inulin)

Taro.explanation: Taro is a starchy root vegetable used in Hawaiian poi and Asian cooking
points: Must be cooked — raw contains calcium oxalate crystals
High in fiber, vitamin E, magnesium
Used in poi (Hawaiian staple), chips, stews
Large leaves also edible when cooked
Major crop in Pacific Islands and Asia

Jicama.explanation: Jicama is a crunchy white root vegetable that tastes like a cross between apple and potato
points: Crisp, juicy, mildly sweet — apple-like texture
High in vitamin C, fiber
Eaten raw in salads, slaws, with lime and chili
Skin is tough — must be peeled
Native to Mexico and Central America

Water Chestnut.explanation: Water chestnuts are crunchy aquatic vegetables that stay crispy even when cooked
points: Corms of aquatic plant — not nuts
Stay crisp when cooked — unique texture
Used in Asian stir-fries, stuffing, salads
Mild sweet flavor
Grown in flooded fields

Lotus Root.explanation: Lotus root has a beautiful lace pattern when sliced and is crunchy to eat
points: Rhizome of lotus plant — decorative holes
Crunchy texture — used in stir-fries, soups
High in vitamin C, fiber
Symbol of purity in Buddhism
Used in Chinese, Japanese, Indian cooking

Daikon.explanation: Daikon is a giant white Japanese radish with a mild flavor
points: Large white radish — can be 20+ inches long
Milder than red radishes
Used in pickles, soups, salads, grated as garnish
High in vitamin C, digestive enzymes
Common in Japanese, Korean, Chinese cuisine

Celeriac.explanation: Celeriac is the root of the celery plant with a mild celery-like flavor
points: Knobby, ugly exterior — smooth white interior
Mild celery flavor — used in soups, mash, remoulade
High in vitamin K, phosphorus
Stores well for months
Popular in European cooking

Samphire.explanation: Samphire is a crunchy sea vegetable that naturally tastes salty
points: Grows in salt marshes — naturally salty flavor
Crunchy succulent texture
High in minerals and omega-3s
Popular in British and European coastal cuisine
Also called sea asparagus

Dandelion Greens.explanation: Dandelion greens are edible and packed with more nutrients than many garden vegetables
points: Extremely nutrient-dense — high in vitamin K, A, C
Bitter flavor — often blanched or cooked
Used in salads, teas, wine
Entire plant edible: leaves, flowers, roots
Considered weed but cultivated in some regions

Nettles.explanation: Stinging nettles sting when raw but lose their sting completely when cooked
points: Stinging hairs contain formic acid — sting disappears when cooked
Very high in iron, calcium, vitamins
Used in soups, teas, pesto
Traditional spring tonic in many cultures
Young leaves best — older become tough

Purslane.explanation: Purslane is a common weed that is actually highly nutritious and edible
points: Highest omega-3 content of any leafy vegetable
Succulent, slightly lemony flavor
High in vitamin A, C, magnesium
Used raw in salads or cooked
Common weed worldwide — often overlooked

Sorrel.explanation: Sorrel has a sour lemony taste because it contains oxalic acid
points: Sharp, lemony flavor from oxalic acid
High in vitamin A, vitamin C
Used in soups, sauces, salads
French sorrel most common variety
Caution: high oxalic acid — moderate consumption

Pak Choi.explanation: Pak choi is a tender Asian green great for quick stir-frying
points: Also called bok choy
Crisp white stems, tender green leaves
High in calcium, vitamin A
Quick cooking — stir-fry, steam, soup
Baby pak choi more tender

Enoki Mushroom.explanation: Enoki mushrooms are long thin white mushrooms with tiny caps
points: Long, thin stems — grown in clusters
Mild flavor — crunchy texture
Used in soups, hot pots, salads
Cultivated in Japan — wild version darker
Low calorie, high in antioxidants

Shiitake.explanation: Shiitake mushrooms have a rich savory flavor and boost the immune system
points: Umami-rich flavor — meaty texture
Contains lentinan — studied for immune support
Used dried or fresh — strong flavor when dried
Cultivated for over 1,000 years in Asia
Second most cultivated mushroom worldwide

Portobello.explanation: Portobello mushrooms are large enough to grill like a burger patty
points: Mature crimini mushroom — large cap
Meaty texture — popular vegetarian burger substitute
Rich, earthy flavor
High in B vitamins, selenium
Gills edible but can darken dishes

Oyster Mushroom.explanation: Oyster mushrooms grow in fan-shaped clusters and have a delicate seafood-like taste
points: Fan or oyster-shaped caps
Mild, slightly seafood-like flavor
Varieties: pearl, pink, yellow, blue
Easy to cultivate — grows on straw, coffee grounds
High in protein and fiber

Truffle.explanation: Truffles are rare underground fungi worth more than gold by weight
points: Grow underground in symbiosis with tree roots
Extremely expensive — white truffles most prized
Strong aroma — used sparingly in cuisine
Hunted with pigs or dogs
Black truffles more common and affordable

Chive.explanation: Chives are the smallest members of the onion family used as a fresh herb garnish
points: Mild onion flavor — used as herb
Edible purple flowers
High in vitamin K
Grows easily in gardens
Common garnish on potatoes, eggs, soups

Shallot.explanation: Shallots taste milder and sweeter than onions and are popular in French cooking
points: Milder, sweeter than regular onions
Used extensively in French and Southeast Asian cooking
Cloves grow in clusters like garlic
High in antioxidants
Delicate flavor — good raw or cooked

Spring Onion.explanation: Spring onions are young onions harvested before the bulb fully forms
points: Also called scallions or green onions
Whole plant edible — mild flavor
Used raw or cooked as garnish
High in vitamin K, vitamin C
Common in Asian, Mexican, and American cuisine

Rapini.explanation: Rapini or broccoli rabe has a pleasantly bitter taste popular in Italian cuisine
points: Bitter flavor — related to turnip, not broccoli
Used in Italian dishes (orecchiette with rapini)
High in vitamin A, vitamin K
Stems, leaves, buds all edible
Quick cooking — blanching reduces bitterness

Fiddlehead Fern.explanation: Fiddlehead ferns are young coiled fern fronds harvested in spring
points: Young coiled fronds — must be cooked
Unique nutty, asparagus-like flavor
High in antioxidants, omega-3s
Seasonal delicacy in spring
Only certain fern species safe to eat

Bamboo Shoot.explanation: Bamboo shoots are young bamboo sprouts eaten as a crunchy vegetable in Asia
points: Young shoots harvested before emerging
Must be cooked to remove bitterness
Crunchy texture — used in stir-fries, soups
High in fiber, low calorie
Major ingredient in Asian cuisine

Galangal.explanation: Galangal looks like ginger but tastes sharper and more piney
points: Related to ginger — harder and more fibrous
Piney, citrusy flavor — used in Thai cooking
Used fresh, dried, or powdered
Medicinal properties in traditional medicine
Greater and lesser varieties

Turmeric.explanation: Turmeric is a bright yellow root that stains everything it touches and is very healthy
points: Contains curcumin — powerful anti-inflammatory compound
Bright yellow color from curcuminoids
Used in curries, golden milk, dyes
Bioavailability increases with black pepper
Ancient medicinal use in Ayurveda

Lemongrass.explanation: Lemongrass is a tropical grass that smells and tastes like fresh lemon
points: Citrusy, lemony flavor — no acidity
Used in Thai, Vietnamese, Indian cooking
Stalks bruised to release oils
Repels insects naturally
Used in teas and essential oils

Bitter Melon.explanation: Bitter melon is a bumpy green vegetable that tastes very bitter but is medicinal
points: Extremely bitter — used to balance sweet dishes
Contains compounds that may help regulate blood sugar
Used in Indian, Chinese, Caribbean cooking
High in vitamin C, antioxidants
Popular in diabetes management in traditional medicine

Moringa.explanation: Moringa leaves are called miracle leaves because they are packed with nutrients
points: Extremely nutrient-dense — high in protein, vitamins, minerals
Leaves, pods, seeds all edible
Used in traditional medicine for centuries
Drought-resistant — grown in arid regions
Called 'drumstick tree' for long pods

Chayote.explanation: Chayote is a pear-shaped green vegetable with a crunchy mild flavor
points: Mild flavor — similar to zucchini/cucumber
Entire fruit edible — seed soft when cooked
High in vitamin C, fiber
Used in Latin American, Asian cooking
Grows on vigorous vines

Plantain.explanation: Plantains look like bananas but are starchy and eaten cooked not raw
points: Starchy — not sweet like dessert bananas
Used green (savory) or ripe (sweet)
Fried, boiled, mashed — tostones, mofongo
Major staple in Africa, Caribbean, Latin America
Higher in potassium than bananas

Yam.explanation: True yams can grow over a meter long and are an important food in West Africa
points: True yams (Dioscorea) different from sweet potatoes
Very large tubers — some over 2 meters long
Starchy staple in West Africa
High in potassium, vitamin C
Boiled, pounded into fufu

Cassava.explanation: Cassava is a starchy root that is the main ingredient in tapioca
points: Major staple in Africa, South America
Must be properly prepared — contains cyanogenic compounds
Source of tapioca starch and pearls
Used in garri, fufu, bread
Drought-tolerant crop

Breadfruit.explanation: Breadfruit is a starchy tropical vegetable that can replace bread and potatoes
points: Starchy fruit — cooked like potato or bread
High in carbohydrates, fiber
Captain Bligh's voyage to transport breadfruit
Used boiled, roasted, fried
Major staple in Pacific Islands

Nopales.explanation: Nopales are the edible pads of the prickly pear cactus popular in Mexico
points: Cactus pads — spines removed
High in fiber, vitamins, antioxidants
Used in salads, tacos, scrambled eggs
Mucilage gives slight slimy texture when cooked
Popular in Mexican cuisine

Calabash.explanation: Calabash is a gourd used as both a vegetable and a natural container
points: Hard shell when mature — used as bottle, bowl
Young fruit eaten as vegetable
Used in Asian, African, Caribbean cooking
Seeds and leaves also edible
Symbol in many cultures

Malanga.explanation: Malanga is a tropical root vegetable with a nutty earthy flavor
points: Related to taro — similar texture
Nutty, earthy flavor
Used in soups, stews, fritters
Popular in Caribbean, Central America
High in starch

Amaranth Leaves.explanation: Amaranth leaves are edible greens from the same plant that produces amaranth grain
points: Highly nutritious — high in vitamins A, C, iron
Used in Indian, African, Caribbean cooking
Called callaloo in Caribbean
Seeds used as grain
Heat-tolerant crop

Kabocha.explanation: Kabocha is a Japanese pumpkin with green skin and very sweet dense flesh
points: Sweet, dry flesh — chestnut-like flavor
Edible skin when cooked
High in beta-carotene, vitamin C
Used in tempura, soups, desserts
Popular in Japan and Korea

Yard Long Bean.explanation: Yard long beans can actually grow up to 18 inches in length
points: Also called asparagus bean
Pods grow very long — 12–18 inches
Used in stir-fries, curries
Mild flavor — similar to green beans
Heat-tolerant legume

Winged Bean.explanation: The winged bean has four frilly wings along its pod and is entirely edible
points: All parts edible: pods, leaves, flowers, tubers
High in protein — called 'poor man's meat'
Pods have four frilly wings
Tropical legume — high yield
Used in Southeast Asian cuisine

Tiger Nut.explanation: Tiger nuts are not nuts but tiny root tubers that are sweet and crunchy
points: Not nut — sedge tuber
Sweet, nutty flavor — crunchy texture
High in fiber, prebiotics
Used in horchata de chufa (Spain)
Ancient food — found in Egyptian tombs

Chinese Broccoli.explanation: Chinese broccoli has thick stems and bitter flat leaves popular in Asian cooking
points: Also called gai lan
Thick stems, blue-green leaves
Slightly bitter — used in stir-fries, oyster sauce
High in vitamin A, vitamin C
Popular in Cantonese cuisine

Sea Beans.explanation: Sea beans grow near the ocean and taste naturally salty without adding salt
points: Also called glasswort or pickleweed
Naturally salty — no added salt needed
Crunchy succulent texture
High in minerals
Used in seafood dishes

Ground Cherry.explanation: Ground cherries are small yellow fruits inside papery husks with a sweet pineapple taste
points: Also called husk cherry
Sweet tropical flavor — pineapple-tomato mix
Ripe when they fall to ground
Used in salads, salsas, desserts
Related to tomatillo

Romanesco Broccoli.explanation: Romanesco broccoli forms a natural fractal spiral pattern and is bright lime green
points: Perfect natural fractal pattern
Milder, nuttier than regular broccoli
High in vitamin C
Visually stunning — gourmet vegetable
Related to cauliflower

Purple Cauliflower.explanation: Purple cauliflower gets its color from anthocyanins the same pigment as blueberries
points: Color from anthocyanins — same as blueberries
Similar nutrition to white cauliflower + antioxidants
Milder flavor than white variety
Vibrant color retained when lightly cooked
Increasingly popular in gourmet markets

Radicchio.explanation: Radicchio is a red leafy vegetable with a pleasantly bitter taste used in Italian salads
points: Bitter flavor — balances rich dishes
Used in Italian salads, risotto, grilled
High in antioxidants
Varieties: Treviso, Chioggia
Related to chicory

Endive.explanation: Endive is a crisp slightly bitter lettuce used in elegant salads and appetizers
points: Crisp, slightly bitter leaves
Belgian endive grown in dark — white/yellow tips
Used in salads, appetizers, braised
High in fiber, vitamin K
Related to chicory and radicchio

Mizuna.explanation: Mizuna is a Japanese mustard green with feathery leaves and a mild peppery taste
points: Feathery leaves — mild mustard flavor
Used in salads, stir-fries, Japanese cuisine
High in vitamin C, antioxidants
Fast-growing salad green
Popular in mesclun mixes

Tatsoi.explanation: Tatsoi forms a beautiful flat rosette of dark spoon-shaped leaves
points: Dark green spoon-shaped leaves
Mild mustard flavor — good raw or cooked
High in calcium, vitamin A
Cold-hardy — grows in fall/winter
Used in Asian cooking

Perilla.explanation: Perilla is a fragrant Asian herb leaf used in Japanese and Korean cooking
points: Also called shiso
Green and red varieties
Aromatic — mint-basil-cinnamon notes
Used as wrap, garnish, in kimchi
High in antioxidants

Agretti.explanation: Agretti is an Italian coastal green tasting slightly salty and resembling chives
points: Also called barba di frate (monk's beard)
Naturally salty flavor
Crunchy succulent texture
Used in Italian salads, pasta
Grows in coastal areas

Scorzonera.explanation: Scorzonera is a black-skinned root vegetable with a mild oyster-like flavor
points: Black skin — white flesh
Mild oyster-like flavor
Used in European cooking
Related to salsify
High in inulin

Salsify.explanation: Salsify is a long white root vegetable nicknamed the oyster plant for its mild taste
points: Oyster-like flavor when cooked
Long black or white roots
Used in soups, roasts
High in inulin
Ancient vegetable — used by Greeks and Romans

Yacon.explanation: Yacon is a South American root that tastes surprisingly sweet like apple and pear
points: Sweet, crisp, juicy — apple-pear flavor
High in fructooligosaccharides — prebiotic
Low calorie — used in weight loss diets
Eaten raw or cooked
Native to Andes

Oca.explanation: Oca is a colorful tuber from the Andes eaten as a potato substitute in South America
points: Brightly colored tubers — red, yellow, pink
Tangy, lemony flavor when raw
Sweetens when exposed to sunlight after harvest
Used boiled, roasted, in salads
Important Andean crop
